narrative: The decision to deny your law school application rests on a prediction that you have a 55.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. That means the model sees you as more likely to fail than to pass, which is simply too high a risk for admission. The most influential factor in this prediction was your class rank in your third year: you placed in the very bottom decile, while accepted students typically sit near the middle of their class. This low standing strongly pushed the model toward predicting bar exam failure. Your first-year rank was also low, but it was your third-year performance that carried the most weight. The second most important factor was your LSAT score, which actually worked in your favor. Your score of 36 is close to the accepted students' average of about 37, and this pushed the prediction toward passing. However, it was not enough to overcome the powerful negative signal from your class rank. The third factor, your family income, had only a small influence. Being in the middle-income bracket nudged the prediction slightly toward failure, but this is a minor consideration and reflects broad patterns rather than your individual ability. In short, the model weighed your near-average LSAT against your consistently low academic standing. Because your college performance suggests a high risk of struggling with the bar exam, your application was denied. To improve your prospects, focus on raising your academic record—perhaps through additional coursework or postgraduate studies that demonstrate your ability to perform at a high level. You could also retake the LSAT, but your strongest signal would be showing that your earlier class ranks were not an accurate reflection of your current potential.
